item.title: Syllabus
item.description:
Introduction to Second Language Acquisition (Postgraduate) #

Note: This syllabus outlines the plan for a 12-week, seminar-style course. Minor adjustments may be made as we progress.

Course website: https://zjpsycholin.github.io/SLA4pg/
Instructor email: jzhang3@ahu.edu.cn

Course Description #

This graduate seminar is a research-oriented introduction to how adults acquire second and additional languages. We emphasize linguistic architecture, cross-linguistic variation, interfaces, processing, and implications for teaching, using Slabakova (2016) as the anchor text. Part I establishes language architecture and variation; Part II situates L2 within broader acquisition contexts and highlights the role of input; Part III surveys adult L2 morphology, syntax, the mental lexicon, interfaces, processing, and classroom implications.

item.title: Ch.1: Language architecture
item.description:
Chapter 1 — Language Architecture & SLA as a Science #

Anchor text: Slabakova, R. (2016). Second Language Acquisition. Chapter 1: Language architecture.
Link to Chapter 1

⭐ Overview #

  • What it means to “know a language” and how that knowledge is organized into parts that work together.
  • How SLA uses the scientific method (observe → generalize → hypothesize → test → revise) to make falsifiable predictions.
  • Why theory-to-evidence links matter (e.g., richer agreement systems may correlate with null subjects) and how this connects to teaching relevance.

🎯 Learning goals #

By the end of Week 1 you should be able to:

item.title: Ch.2: Language Variation
item.description:
Chapter 2 — Language Variation & the Learning Task" #

Anchor text: Slabakova, R. (2016). Second Language Acquisition. Chapter 2: Language variation.
Link to Chapter 2

⭐ Overview #

  • How languages differ and what that means for learning a second language.
  • Where variation “lives” in the grammar today (hint: features in the functional lexicon) and why that matters for learners.
  • How prior knowledge from the L1 transfers into the L2 starting point, and what “resetting” involves.
  • Why some areas (e.g., functional morphology and mismatched feature cues) tend to be harder.

🎯 Learning goals #

By the end of Week 2 you should be able to:

item.title: Ch.3: The Psychological Reality of Language in Use
item.description:
Chapter 3 — The Psychological Reality of Language in Use #

Anchor text: Slabakova, R. (2016). Second Language Acquisition. Chapter 3: The psychological reality of language in use.
Link to Chapter 3

⭐ Overview #

  • What “processing” means: how the mind builds meaning in real time during listening/reading and plans forms during speaking.
  • Big ideas: the parser, timing, limited resources, and why learners sometimes rely on easier cues (semantics/discourse) over costly structure when time is tight.
  • What common methods actually measure (self-paced reading, eye-tracking, ERP) and how to read their basic signals.
  • Why this matters: classroom input and tasks can shape processing (e.g., highlighting small forms, pacing, repeated exposure).

🎯 Learning goals #

By the end of Week 3 you should be able to:

item.title: Ch.4: The Critical Period Hypothesis (CPH)
item.description:
Chapter 4 — The Critical Period Hypothesis (CPH) #

Anchor text: Slabakova, R. (2016). Second Language Acquisition. Chapter 4: The Critical Period Hypothesis.
Link to Chapter 4

⭐ Overview #

  • What the Critical Period Hypothesis (CPH) claims and why age might matter for language learning.
  • How age of acquisition (AoA) interacts with input amount/quality, use, and education.
  • Why age effects differ across subsystems: phonology (accent) vs. morphosyntax/semantics (mixed evidence).
  • What counts as persuasive evidence (tasks, outcomes, controls) and what would falsify a strong CPH claim.

🎯 Learning goals #

By the end of Week 4 you should be able to:

item.title: Questionset1
item.description:
After-Class Research Task: Analyzing Real Second Language Morphosyntactic Data #

A Mini Research Project on Interlanguage Morphosyntax** #

Deadline: April 17th, 2026 #

Task Overview #

In this task, you will carry out a small-scale second language acquisition (SLA) research project based on real learner data. Your goal is to collect, organize, and analyze authentic second language data in order to identify morphosyntactic patterns, formulate generalizations, and develop theoretically informed hypotheses about learner knowledge and interlanguage development.

item.title: Ch.8: Acquisition of Syntax
item.description:
Chapter 8 — Acquisition of Syntax #

Anchor text: Slabakova, R. (2016). Second Language Acquisition. Chapter 8: Acquisition of Syntax.
Link to Chapter 8

Readings

  • Failed Functional Features Hypothesis
    • Hawkins and Chan (1997) Link to Text
  • Verb Movement
    • White (1990) Link to Text
  • Wh-movement
    • Belikova and White (2009) Link to Text

1. Pre-Class Preview Guide #

1.1 Chapter Core Focus #

This chapter explores the acquisition of syntax (sentence structure and grammatical dependencies) in second language (L2) learning, with a focus on three core themes: how the concept of “syntactic parameters” has evolved, whether L2 learners develop native-like syntactic representations, and how cross-linguistic differences (e.g., word order, verb movement, wh-movement) shape acquisition.

item.title: Ch.10: Acquisition of the Syntax-Semantics Interface
item.description:
Chapter 10 — Acquisition of the Syntax-Semantics Interface #

Anchor text: Slabakova, R. (2016). Second Language Acquisition. Chapter 10: Acquisition of the Syntax–Semantics Interface.
Link to Chapter 10

Readings

  • grammatical aspect
    • Slabakova (2003) Link to Text
  • POS at the syntax-semantics interface
    • Marsden (2009) Link to Text
  • Discontunuous interrogatives
    • Dekydtspotter and Sprouse (2001) Link to Text

⭐ Overview #

  • The five key types of meaning in language: lexical, phrasal (sentential) semantic, grammatical, discourse-related, and pragmatic—and how they interact with syntax .
  • Syntax–semantics mismatches: When universal meanings (e.g., ongoing/habitual events) are encoded by different forms across languages (e.g., English past progressive vs. Spanish Imperfect) .
  • Poverty of the Stimulus (POS) in semantics: How L2 learners acquire meanings not attested in input (e.g., missing interpretations of impersonal se in Spanish preterit) .
  • Special learning challenges: novel constructions (e.g., French discontinuous interrogatives) and morphologically unmarked meanings (e.g., English articles for Russian/Korean learners) .

🎯 Learning goals #

By the end of Week 10 you should be able to:

item.title: Ch.11: Acquisition of the Syntax-Discourse & Semantics-Pragmatics Interfaces
item.description:
<!-- ## Chapter 11 — Acquisition of the Syntax-Discourse & Semantics-Pragmatics Interfaces
**Anchor text**: Slabakova, R. (2016). *Second Language Acquisition*. **Chapter 11: Acquisition of the Syntax–Discourse and Semantics–Pragmatics Interfaces**. [Link to Chapter 11](/SLA4pg/pdfs/C11_syntax-disc_sem-prag.pdf)
**Readings** - Shallow Structure Hypothesis - Clahsen and Felser (2006) [Link to Text](/SLA4pg/pdfs/ClahsenFelser2006.pdf) - Plausibility in L2 language processing - Roberts and Felser (2011) [Link to Text](/SLA4pg/pdfs/RobertsFelser2011.pdf)
### ⭐ Overview - The two key external interfaces: 1. **Syntax–Discourse Interface**: How syntax encodes discourse information (e.g., Topic/Focus via word order, clitics) . 2. **Semantics–Pragmatics Interface**: How context and universal pragmatic principles (e.g., Gricean maxims) adjust literal meaning (e.g., scalar implicatures) . - Why interface properties are often harder to acquire: They require integrating linguistic (syntax/semantics) and extralinguistic (context/culture) information—taxing working memory . - Key phenomena: **Topic/Focus marking** (clitic doubling, word order), **pronoun reference** (null/overt pronoun division of labor), **intonation as discourse cue**, and **scalar implicatures** .
### 🎯 Learning goals By the end of Week 11 you should be able to: 1. Distinguish the **syntax–discourse interface** (e.g., clitic doubling for Topic) from the **semantics–pragmatics interface** (e.g., scalar implicatures) and explain why both rely on context . 2. Describe how languages mark Topic/Focus (e.g., English topicalization vs. Spanish clitic left dislocation) and predict L2 acquisition challenges . 3. Apply the **Interface Hypothesis** to explain why near-native learners struggle with pronoun reference (e.g., Italian overt pronouns for Topic shift) . 4. Explain why scalar implicatures (e.g., *some* = "not all") are universal but may still be processed differently in L2—especially under cognitive load .
---
### 📖 Reading (do before class) - **Required**: Slabakova (2016), **Chapter 11** (focus on Sections 11.1–11.6; prioritize interface definitions and key phenomena over technical exercises). - As you read, note: - How L1 transfer affects interface acquisition (e.g., Turkish learners of Dutch transferring null pronoun reference rules) . - Why frequency of interface constructions (e.g., English topicalization is rare) impacts learning success .
**Guiding questions while you read** 1. Why do Spanish learners of English struggle with topicalization (*The wine she didn’t drink* vs. *The wine she didn’t drink it*)? 2. How do Italian native speakers use null vs. overt pronouns to signal Topic maintenance vs. Topic shift? 3. Why do adult L2 learners compute scalar implicatures more accurately than L1 children but less consistently than L1 adults?
---
### 🧠 Key terms *syntax–discourse interface; semantics–pragmatics interface; Topic; Focus (presentational/contrastive); clitic doubling; topicalization; Interface Hypothesis; pronoun reference (division of labor); intonation (nuclear stress); scalar implicatures; Gricean maxims (Quantity Maxim); deaccenting*
---
## CHAPTER 11: ACQUISITION OF THE SYNTAX–DISCOURSE & SEMANTICS–PRAGMATICS INTERFACES **Core Goal**: Understand how L2 learners integrate syntax/semantics with discourse context and pragmatic principles—and why these interfaces are uniquely challenging.
### 11.1 Defining the Interfaces External interfaces connect core grammar to context—unlike internal interfaces (e.g., syntax–semantics) which are language-internal:
| Interface | Core Function | Key Phenomena | |-----------|---------------|---------------| | **Syntax–Discourse** | Encodes discourse status (Topic = old info; Focus = new info) via syntax | Clitic doubling, topicalization, VS word order, pronoun reference | | **Semantics–Pragmatics** | Adjusts literal (semantic) meaning via context/world knowledge | Scalar implicatures, deixis (*this/that*), anaphoric deaccenting |
- **Key Distinction**: Syntax–discourse relies on *prior discourse* (e.g., "The wine" = Topic because it was mentioned earlier); semantics–pragmatics relies on *universal principles* (e.g., Grice’s Quantity Maxim) .
### 11.2 Marking Topic & Focus Across Languages Languages use different syntactic strategies to signal Topic (old info) and Focus (new info)—mismatches between L1 and L2 create acquisition challenges:
#### 1. Clitic Doubling for Topic - **Spanish/Bulgarian**: Topicalized objects require a clitic pronoun (doubling) to signal old info. Example: - Spanish: *A Pedro, no lo saludó* ("Pedro, I didn’t greet him") → *lo* = clitic doubling Topic *Pedro* . - Bulgarian: *Vinoto tja ne *(go) pi* ("The wine she didn’t drink it") → *go* = mandatory clitic for Topic *vinoto* . - **English**: Topicalized objects *forbid* resumptive pronouns: *The wine she didn’t drink (*it)* . - **Acquisition Findings**: - Advanced English learners of Bulgarian master clitic doubling for Topic (Ivanov 2009) . - Spanish learners of English struggle to omit resumptive pronouns in topicalization (Slabakova & García Mayo 2015)—due to English topicalization’s rarity in input .
#### 2. Word Order for Focus - **Spanish (null-subject language)**: VS word order signals presentational Focus (new info): - Q: *¿Quién gritó?* ("Who shouted?") → A: *Gritó una mujer* ("Shouted a woman") . - Neutral context (out of blue): VS preferred for unaccusative verbs (*Vino la policía* = "Arrived the police") but not unergative verbs (*Una mujer gritó* = "A woman shouted") . - **English**: Fixed SV order; Focus marked via intonation (e.g., *A WOMAN shouted*) . - **Acquisition Findings**: - English learners of Spanish master SV/VS distinction for unaccusative/unergative verbs but fail to link VS to Focus (Lozano 2006)—supports the **Interface Hypothesis** (discourse integration is taxing) .
### 11.3 Pronoun Reference at the Syntax–Discourse Interface Null and overt pronouns have a "division of labor" in discourse—this is a classic interface property:
#### 1. Romance Languages (Spanish/Italian) - **Null Pronouns**: Signal **Topic maintenance** (embedded subject = main clause subject). Example: - Italian: *La vecchietta saluta la ragazza quando attraversa la strada* ("The old lady greets the girl when [she] crosses the street") → *attraversa* = null pronoun = old Topic (la vecchietta) . - **Overt Pronouns**: Signal **Topic shift** (embedded subject = new referent). Example: - Italian: *La vecchietta saluta la ragazza quando lei attraversa la strada* ("The old lady greets the girl when she crosses the street") → *lei* = overt pronoun = new referent (la ragazza) .
#### 2. L2 Acquisition Challenges - **Near-Native Learners**: Less sensitive to Topic shift—30% of Italian near-natives interpret overt pronouns as Topic maintenance (vs. 5% of natives) (Belletti et al. 2007) . - **Heritage Speakers**: May never acquire the division of labor (Shin & Cairns 2009)—exposed to English before age 7 (when Topic shift sensitivity emerges in L1) . - **Chinese Learners of English**: Master null object reference (e.g., *Xiao Zhang says Lao Wang likes ø*) by advanced proficiency—showing interface success is possible with clear input .
### 11.4 Intonation as a Discourse Cue Intonation (nuclear stress, deaccenting) signals Focus/Topic—but L1 prosodic rules transfer and complicate L2 learning:
#### 1. English vs. Spanish Prosody - **English**: Nuclear Stress (NS) is flexible—marks Focus on any constituent. Example: - Q: *Who broke his leg?* → A: *A BOY broke his leg* (NS on Focus *boy*) . - **Anaphoric Deaccenting**: Old info loses stress (e.g., Q: *Why buy that stamp?* → A: *Because I COLLECT stamps*—NS shifts to *collect* because *stamps* is old info) . - **Spanish**: NS is fixed (last constituent) — Focus marked via word order (not intonation) .
#### 2. Acquisition Findings - Spanish learners of English acquire **deaccenting** (new rule) before restructuring **NS** (L1 transfer) (Nava & Zubizarreta 2009) . - Advanced learners still struggle with NS flexibility—prefer L1-like fixed stress (Zubizarreta & Nava 2011) .
### 11.5 Scalar Implicatures at the Semantics–Pragmatics Interface Scalar implicatures (e.g., *some* = "not all") are universal but require cognitive effort—explaining L2 processing differences:
#### 1. How Implicatures Work - **Logical Meaning**: *Some professors are smart* = "some and possibly all" . - **Pragmatic Meaning**: *Some professors are smart* = "not all professors are smart" (via Grice’s Quantity Maxim: "Be as informative as required") .
#### 2. L2 Acquisition Findings - **Universal Mechanisms**: Korean learners of English compute implicatures at 60% (vs. natives’ 40%) in L2—better than L1 children (Slabakova 2010) . - **Processing Load**: Learners struggle with *indirect implicatures* (e.g., *Max didn’t read all the books* = "Max read some")—more cognitively demanding than direct implicatures (Lieberman 2009) . - **Bilingual Advantage**: Bilingual children outperform monolinguals on Gricean maxims (relevance, politeness) but not on scalar implicatures—suggests different processing demands (Siegal et al. 2009) .
### 11.6 The Interface Hypothesis & Key Conclusions - **Interface Hypothesis (Sorace 2011)**: External interfaces (syntax–discourse, semantics–pragmatics) are more vulnerable than internal interfaces—due to working memory strain from integrating linguistic/contextual info . - **Nuance**: Interface difficulty is not universal—frequency of constructions matters: - Spanish clitic left dislocation (common) is acquired easily; English topicalization (rare) is not (Slabakova 2015) . - **Final Takeaways**: 1. Syntax–discourse properties require matching L2 syntax to discourse context—challenged by L1 transfer and input rarity . 2. Semantics–pragmatics properties (implicatures) are universal but taxed by L2 processing load . 3. Near-native learners may show residual optionality at interfaces—but success is possible with sufficient input .
### Preview/Review Questions #### Preview 1. What is the difference between "Topic maintenance" and "Topic shift"? How do pronouns signal this? 2. Why is anaphoric deaccenting (English) harder for Spanish learners than deaccenting (Spanish)?
#### Review 1. How does the Interface Hypothesis explain why near-native Italian learners misinterpret overt pronouns? 2. Why do English learners of Spanish master VS word order for unaccusative verbs but not for Focus? 3. What evidence shows scalar implicatures are universal but cognitively demanding in L2?
-->

item.title: Ch 12: L2 Processing
item.description:
Chapter 12: L2 Processing – Student Study Guide #

Source: Slabakova, R. (2016). Second Language Acquisition. Chapter 12.

What Is This Chapter About? #

In earlier chapters, we focused on what L2 learners know about grammar (representations).
This chapter shifts to how L2 learners use that knowledge in real time (processing).

Big question: Do L2 learners process language in the same way as native speakers, or in a fundamentally different way?

item.title: Term Research Proposal Guidelines: Generative Second Language Acquisition (SLA)
item.description:
Term Research Proposal Guidelines #

Generative Second Language Acquisition (SLA) #

1. Overview #

This assignment requires you to design a small-scale original research proposal grounded in generative approaches to SLA. Your proposal should identify a clear theoretical problem in generative SLA, formulate well-defined research questions, and outline a methodologically appropriate study informed by existing generative literature. The goal is to demonstrate your ability to connect generative theory with empirical research design.
